subject.title: A Boat Beneath a Sunny Sky
subject.author: Lewis Carroll
subject.text:
A boat beneath a sunny sky,
Lingering onward dreamily
In an evening of July -

Children three that nestle near,
Eager eye and willing ear,
Pleased a simple tale to hear -

Long has paled that sunny sky:
Echoes fade and memories die:
Autumn frosts have slain July.

Still she haunts me, phantomwise,
Alice moving under skies
Never seen by waking eyes.

Children yet, the tale to hear,
Eager eye and willing ear,
Lovingly shall nestle near.

In a Wonderland they lie,
Dreaming as the days go by,
Dreaming as the summers die:

Ever drifting down the stream -
Lingering in the golden gleam -
Life, what is it but a dream?

title: The Only Place Carroll Wrote Her Full Name
standfirst: Twenty-one lines close Through the Looking-Glass, and their first letters spell ALICE PLEASANCE LIDDELL — the only time in either Alice book Carroll wrote her full name outright. He did it three years after an unexplained break with her family, and deep into years of publicly denying she was ever the model for his heroine.

sections.heading: The Sunny Sky Nobody Can Confirm
sections.body:
"A boat beneath a sunny sky, / Lingering onward dreamily / In an evening of July -" So the poem opens, dating the afternoon it commemorates precisely: 4 July 1862, when Charles Dodgson and a young Christ Church clergyman, [Robinson Duckworth](https://sites.utexas.edu/ransomcentermagazine/2015/07/02/july-4-1862-a-golden-afternoon-with-alice-and-her-sisters/), rowed three of Dean Henry Liddell's daughters five miles up the Isis from Folly Bridge to [Godstow](https://blog.bookstellyouwhy.com/who-really-inspired-lewis-carrolls-alice-characters), telling them along the way the story that became Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

Whether the sky was actually sunny is not settled. Alice herself later described a burning heat that sent the party looking for shade under haystacks near Godstow. Carroll's biographers, [checking the Oxford weather records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_in_the_golden_afternoon...) against that account, found a different day: cloudy, rain-touched, nothing golden about it — though the claim has [been disputed since](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_in_the_golden_afternoon...) too. Nobody now can settle which memory was right. What's certain is that nine years later, this poem's opening lines were built on a recollection even the people who lived it couldn't agree on.

sections.heading: Twenty-One Lines, One Name
sections.body:
Read down the first letter of each of the poem's twenty-one lines — A, L, I, C, E, P, L, E, A, S, A, N, C, E, L, I, D, D, E, L, L — and they spell ALICE PLEASANCE LIDDELL, the [full name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Liddell) of the child who had asked, nine years before, to have the boat-trip story written down. Nothing on the page announces the trick. Read normally, the poem is a complete, grammatical piece about memory and loss, and most readers finish it without ever checking the margin, because the pattern doesn't survive being read aloud, translated, or reset in a different typeface — it exists only in that one column of first letters, exactly as printed.

It wasn't a one-off gesture. Carroll had [a lifelong taste for wordplay, logic games and acrostics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Carroll), and used the form for other children he knew too. But this is the only acrostic built into either Alice book, and the only place across nine years of writing about her that he set down Alice Liddell's whole legal name at all.

sections.heading: A Name He'd Spent Years Denying
sections.body: By December 1871, when Through the Looking-Glass reached print, [Dodgson had made a public habit of denying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Carroll) that his fictional Alice was modelled on any real child — this despite a family connection assumed by nearly everyone who knew the Liddells, and later treated as settled fact by his own biographers. It is an odd position to hold while closing the same book with the real girl's actual name, spelled out letter by letter for anyone patient enough to check. The acrostic doesn't expose the denial as a lie exactly; a fictional heroine and a private tribute could coexist without contradiction. But it does show a writer choosing, quite deliberately, where the name he wouldn't say in public was allowed to live: not in an interview, not in a preface, but inside a form built so that almost nobody would read it as a name being said at all.

sections.heading: Half a Life Asunder
sections.body:
The same book that hides Alice's name at the end addresses her, unmistakably though never by name, at the start. [Through the Looking-Glass opens with its own dedication poem](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/12/12-h/12-h.htm), six years after Wonderland's, and in a far less playful register:

> Child of the pure unclouded brow
> And dreaming eyes of wonder!
> Though time be fleet, and I and thou
> Are half a life asunder,

A few lines later it turns starker still: "I have not seen thy sunny face, / Nor heard thy silver laughter; / No thought of me shall find a place / In thy young life's hereafter."

That distance had a specific cause. In June 1863, something happened between Dodgson and the [Liddell family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Liddell) that neither side explained in anything that survives — a diary page for those exact days is one of several missing from Dodgson's journals, and a note attributed to his niece mentions gossip involving the family's governess and Alice's sister Lorina. Whatever it was, it ended the closeness of 1862. By 1871 the dedication poem admits, in plain words, that he no longer expects to see her face or hear her laugh. The acrostic on the book's last page admits nothing so directly. It just writes her name where the poem gets to stay silent about what that name still means.

sections.heading: Scores of Child-Friends Since
sections.body:
Alice Liddell's later life ran mostly separate from Carroll's. She [married the cricketer Reginald Hargreaves in 1880](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Liddell) at Westminster Abbey, had three sons, and lost two of them in the First World War. When Carroll wrote to her as an adult, the warmth was real but plainly filed under the past: "I have had some scores of child-friends since your time," he told her, "[but they have been quite a different thing](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/07/04/story-of-alice/)." Your time, not our time — a friendship he had already moved into history.

After Hargreaves died in 1926, financial pressure led Alice to sell the original manuscript of Alice's Adventures Under Ground; it went at Sotheby's for £15,400, nearly four times the reserve price. In 1932, at eighty, she travelled to Columbia University for the centenary of Carroll's birth and watched her own childhood manuscript displayed as a historical artefact. By then the acrostic closing Through the Looking-Glass had been sitting in print, unremarked, for over sixty years — the one place Carroll had actually written her whole name, inside a book most of its readers finished without ever noticing it was there.

sections.heading: The Question the Poem Never Answers
sections.body: The poem's last line asks, "Life, what is it but a dream?" Read against everything the poem is built from, that lands less like whimsy and more like an honest admission. The sunny afternoon it opens on is a memory even the people who were there couldn't agree on. The name running down its margin is the one name Carroll spent years publicly refusing to attach to his fiction, written here so carefully that it required active decoding rather than reading. And it closes a book whose own opening poem had already conceded, in plain language, that the child it addressed was years and one unexplained rupture away from the girl in the boat. A poem built this precisely, carrying a real person's real name with that much care, and ending on a question about whether any of it was solid to begin with — that isn't uncertainty for effect. It's the one form of honesty the poem had left to give.
